title: Compromise Accounts
summary: Where establishment builds a new identity, compromise takes over one that already exists, and the difference matters because an existing identity arrives with history, contacts and reputation that no new account can fake quickly. Access is usually bought or guessed rather than broken: credential dumps from unrelated breaches, reused passwords, password spraying against services without lockout, phishing pages, and in some cases payment to an insider. Once inside, the adversary often reshapes the account with forwarding rules, new recovery addresses and profile edits so the persona supports the next stage. The defensive signature is a change in behaviour for a known identity rather than a suspicious destination.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker takes over an account that already belongs to someone else. They do not make a new one. They use the trust that the real account already has. The account might belong to a person, a company or a supplier. Because it looks genuine, the people who receive messages from it are less suspicious. The hard part for defenders is that the name on the account is correct.
beginner.whyItMatters: A stolen account can send messages that look completely normal to friends, colleagues and customers. The recipient sees a familiar name and a real address. Attackers also use the account to learn about the organisation, because old mail holds plans, invoices and contacts. Resetting one password is often not enough, since the attacker may have added a forwarding rule or a new recovery address. If the account belongs to a supplier, that trust can carry into your own network. Fast detection of unusual account behaviour limits the damage.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains a password, often from a breach at an unrelated website.
They sign in with that password, especially where the same password is reused.
They add their own recovery address or mailbox rule to keep quiet access.
They read old messages to learn about the organisation and its contacts.
They then send messages or request payments while pretending to be the owner.
If challenged, they may edit the profile to match the story they tell.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk. Guests trust the person behind it because the uniform and the desk are familiar. If someone steals a uniform and stands at the desk, guests hand over key cards and room numbers without thinking. The thief never broke a lock. They borrowed the look of authority. A compromised account works the same way. The attacker wears the identity of someone you already know and uses the trust you already gave that person.
takeaways: A familiar sender is not proof that the message is genuine.
Check mailbox rules and recovery settings after any suspected takeover.
Unique passwords stop one breach from opening many accounts.

objectives: Explain how compromised accounts differ from newly created accounts.
List common ways that attackers obtain working credentials.
Identify account changes that suggest a takeover is in progress.
Describe how a hijacked account supports phishing and payment fraud.
Recommend response steps for a suspected account compromise.
